overview: This domain covers the agency that enforces the Sarbanes-Oxley Act and the tools around it: the two securities laws the SEC administers, how it writes rules, and how its investigations, settlements and referrals work. It then covers the Act's records and fraud crimes, protections and rewards for whistleblowers, and the Dodd-Frank Act of 2010, which created new financial stability bodies and amended SOX.
analogy: Think of a national sports league. Its founding rulebooks say how players join and how games are played, and the league office writes new rules after asking teams for comments. The office investigates fouls, warns players before charging them and can fine or suspend, but only the police can arrest. Tampering with game footage is a separate crime, and players who report cheating are protected and can be rewarded. After a scandal, a reform law adds a safety council and updates some old rules.

topics.topic_name: The Securities Act and the Exchange Act
topics.overview: The two founding securities laws split the work: the 1933 Act governs offerings, and the 1934 Act created the SEC and governs trading, market firms and periodic reports. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act sits on top of them, and the SEC enforces it as part of the Exchange Act.
can_do: Tell which Act governs an offering and which governs trading and reporting
Name the Act that created the SEC
Explain how a SOX violation is enforced through the Exchange Act

subtopics.name: The Securities Act of 1933
subtopics.definition: The Securities Act of 1933 is the federal law that governs offers and sales of securities, requiring registration and disclosure and banning fraud in sales.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is the entry gate to U.S. public markets: before a company sells securities to the public, investors must get the facts. Mixing it up with the 1934 Act is a classic exam trap.
how_it_works: The SEC calls it the 'truth in securities' law, with two aims: give investors key facts about offered securities and ban fraud in their sale.
Section 5 (15 U.S.C. 77e) bars offering or selling a security through the mails or interstate commerce unless a registration statement is filed or in effect.
Registration forms describe the business, the security, management and financial statements certified by independent accountants.
Some offerings are exempt, such as private offerings to a limited number of investors, limited-size or intrastate offerings, and government securities.
The SEC requires accurate disclosure but does not guarantee it or judge whether a security is a good investment.

rows.label: Main subject
cells: Trading, market firms and reporting after issue

rows.label: Key duty
cells: Register the offering and deliver a prospectus
File periodic reports; register exchanges and brokers

subtopics.example: Brightwell Foods plans to raise money by selling new bonds to the public. Its treasurer, Ana, assumes the company's existing annual reports cover the sale. Outside counsel explains that the bond offering needs its own registration statement and prospectus under the 1933 Act unless an exemption applies, and the team starts drafting the filing.

review: Compare each planned offering with the registration duty and the exemptions
Trace prospectus figures to the audited numbers they come from
evidence: EDGAR filing record for each offering document
Legal opinion supporting any exemption claimed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the finance team and counsel confirm registration or an exemption before any offer is made.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the offering; counsel advises on registration

subtopics.isaca_rule: A new offer or sale of securities points to the 1933 Act: register it or rely on an exemption, and never mislead buyers. Trading, market firms and periodic reports after issue belong to the 1934 Act.

exam_traps.trap: SEC registration means the SEC vouches for the investment.
exam_traps.why: The SEC requires accurate disclosure but does not guarantee it; investors make their own judgment about the security.

exam_traps.trap: Every sale of securities must be registered.
exam_traps.why: Exemptions exist, such as private offerings to a limited number of persons, limited-size and intrastate offerings, and government securities.

key_terms.definition: The disclosure document an issuer files with the SEC before offering securities, covering the business, the security, management and finances.
The offering document given to investors, drawn from the registration statement.
An offering the law lets a company make without registering, such as a private offering.

subtopics.memory_aid: 1933: the first sale. Register it or find an exemption.

subtopics.name: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934
subtopics.definition: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 created the SEC and governs securities trading, exchanges, brokers and the periodic reports of companies with publicly traded securities.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most SOX duties attach to companies that report under this Act, and SOX is enforced through it. Knowing which Act applies tells you who must comply and how violations are pursued.
how_it_works: Section 4 (15 U.S.C. 78d) established the Securities and Exchange Commission, with five commissioners appointed by the President with Senate consent.
The Act lets the SEC register, regulate and oversee exchanges, brokers, transfer agents, clearing agencies and self-regulatory organizations such as FINRA.
It requires periodic reports from companies with publicly traded securities and covers proxy solicitations, tender offers and insider trading.
SOX Section 3(b) treats a violation of SOX, an SEC rule under it or a PCAOB rule like an Exchange Act violation, with the same penalties.
So SOX did not replace the 1933 or 1934 Act; it added duties that the SEC enforces with its existing powers.
subtopics.example: Harbor Logistics already has listed shares. A new director, Sam, asks whether SOX replaced the old securities laws. The general counsel explains that the company still files annual and quarterly reports under the 1934 Act, and that SOX duties such as officer certifications sit on top of those reports.

review: Confirm which periodic reports the company must file under the Exchange Act
Map each SOX duty to the Exchange Act report it attaches to
evidence: Filing history on EDGAR showing timely annual and quarterly reports
Disclosure calendar listing report deadlines and SOX steps
audit_focus.recommend: Have the disclosure committee track Exchange Act filings and the SOX duties attached to each report.
audit_focus.decides: The CEO and CFO answer for the reports they certify

subtopics.isaca_rule: The 1934 Act created the SEC and governs what happens after issue: trading, market firms and periodic reports. A SOX violation is enforced as an Exchange Act violation (SOX Section 3(b)).

exam_traps.trap: The Securities Act of 1933 created the SEC.
exam_traps.why: The SEC was established by Section 4 of the 1934 Act (15 U.S.C. 78d). The 1933 Act governs offerings.

exam_traps.trap: SOX replaced the 1933 and 1934 Acts.
exam_traps.why: SOX added duties on top of them, and Section 3(b) enforces SOX violations as Exchange Act violations, so both older Acts remain in force.

key_terms.definition: A body such as an exchange or FINRA that writes and enforces rules for its members under SEC oversight.
The annual, quarterly and current reports that companies with publicly traded securities file under the Exchange Act.

subtopics.memory_aid: 1934: the SEC is born, and trading and reports follow.

topics.overview: Much of SOX works through SEC rules rather than the statute's own words. This topic covers how the SEC adopts a rule, from public proposal to effective date, and how SOX sections direct the rules that set the detailed duties.
can_do: Put the steps of notice-and-comment rulemaking in order
Tell when a rule binds companies: proposed, adopted or effective
Find the SEC rule behind a SOX section, such as Rule 2-06 behind Section 802

subtopics.name: Notice-and-Comment Rulemaking
subtopics.definition: Notice-and-comment rulemaking is the process by which the SEC proposes a rule publicly, takes comments, and then adopts a final rule with its reasons.
subtopics.why_it_matters: SEC rules carry the force of law, and many SOX duties work through them. Knowing the steps tells you whether a rule is only proposed, adopted, or already binding.
how_it_works: The SEC publishes a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register, with the rule's terms or subjects and its legal authority (5 U.S.C. 553(b)).
Interested persons submit written data, views or arguments, which the SEC considers before adopting the rule (553(c)).
The final rule includes a concise general statement of its basis and purpose (553(c)).
A substantive rule is published at least 30 days before its effective date, unless an exception applies (553(d)).
Interpretive rules, policy statements, procedural rules, or a stated good-cause finding can skip notice and comment (553(b)).
Anyone may petition the SEC to issue, amend or repeal a rule (553(e)).
subtopics.example: A trade group reads an SEC proposal for a new disclosure item in the Federal Register. Its policy director, Lee, files a comment letter with cost data before the deadline. Months later the SEC adopts a revised final rule whose release explains which comments changed the text and sets an effective date.

review: Inspect the rule tracker for proposals that affect the company's filings
Compare the company's adoption plan with the rule's compliance dates
evidence: Rule tracker entries with owners and compliance dates
Comment letters the company filed, if any
audit_focus.recommend: Have the legal team monitor proposed SEC rules and plan compliance from each final rule's effective date.
audit_focus.decides: The Commission votes to adopt final rules; management plans compliance

subtopics.isaca_rule: A substantive SEC rule goes from proposal to comment to a final rule with reasons, then takes effect at least 30 days later (5 U.S.C. 553). A statute telling the SEC to act says what to adopt, not that comment can be skipped.

exam_traps.trap: Once Congress orders a rule, the SEC can adopt it without public comment.
exam_traps.why: Section 553 still applies unless an exception fits, such as an interpretive rule or a good-cause finding the agency states in the rule.

exam_traps.trap: A proposed rule binds companies from the day it is published.
exam_traps.why: Only a final rule binds, and a substantive rule generally takes effect at least 30 days after it is published.

key_terms.definition: The U.S. government's daily publication of proposed and final agency rules and notices.
An agency finding, stated in the rule, that notice and comment are impracticable, unnecessary or contrary to the public interest.

subtopics.memory_aid: Propose, comment, adopt, wait: then the rule binds.

subtopics.name: Rules the Sarbanes-Oxley Act Directed
subtopics.definition: Many SOX duties take effect through SEC rules: the Act tells the SEC to write rules, and those rules set the detailed requirements companies and auditors follow.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The right answer often names the rule, not only the section. Knowing that a section works through a rule tells you where the detail lives and who enforces it.
how_it_works: Section 3(a) lets the SEC adopt rules needed in the public interest, to protect investors or to carry out the Act.
Some sections set deadlines: 18 U.S.C. 1520(a)(2), from Section 802, told the SEC to adopt audit record rules within 180 days, after notice and comment.
The SEC's retention rule is Rule 2-06 of Regulation S-X (17 CFR 210.2-06, published 30 Jan 2003), which sets a seven-year period.
Section 404(a) names management's responsibility and assessment, then directs SEC rules; Item 308(a) (17 CFR 229.308(a), opened 31 Oct 2026) sets the full contents.
No PCAOB rule takes effect without prior SEC approval (SOX Section 107(b)); the SEC oversees the PCAOB, not the reverse.
subtopics.example: Morgan, a new compliance analyst at Tidewater Health, finds Section 404(a) in the Act but cannot find what management's report must contain. Their manager shows them the SEC's rules in Regulation S-K, which list the report's contents, and explains that the Act set the duty while the rule supplies the detail.

review: Map each SOX section the company relies on to its implementing SEC rule
Compare internal policies with the current rule text, not only the statute
evidence: Rule-to-policy map naming each CFR section and its owner
Dated copies of each implementing rule as last reviewed
audit_focus.recommend: Have the compliance team cite the implementing SEC rule for each SOX duty in internal policies.
audit_focus.decides: Management complies with the rules the SEC writes and enforces

subtopics.isaca_rule: When a SOX section tells the SEC to prescribe rules, the duty in practice is the rule's text. Cite both the section and the rule, check the current CFR, and remember that PCAOB rules need SEC approval.

exam_traps.trap: The statute alone tells you everything a company or auditor must do.
exam_traps.why: Many sections only direct rulemaking; the detail, such as Rule 2-06's seven-year period, sits in the SEC's rules.

exam_traps.trap: Rule 2-06 is a PCAOB auditing standard.
exam_traps.why: It is an SEC rule in Regulation S-X (17 CFR 210.2-06), though it points to PCAOB and SEC standards for what workpapers contain.

key_terms.definition: The SEC's rules on the form and content of financial statements, including Rule 2-06 on audit record retention.
The SEC's rules on non-financial disclosure in filings, including management's internal control report.

subtopics.memory_aid: The Act sets the duty; the rule sets the detail.

topics.overview: An SEC enforcement matter moves from inquiry to investigation, may bring a Wells notice, and ends in a civil action, an administrative proceeding, a settlement, a referral or a closing. Along the way the company must decide what to disclose and must preserve its records.
can_do: Tell a voluntary request from a subpoena under a formal order
Explain what a Wells notice is and is not
Name what an SEC settlement can and cannot resolve
Separate the duty to preserve records from the judgment on disclosure

subtopics.name: Inquiries, Investigations and Formal Orders
subtopics.definition: An SEC enforcement matter starts as a matter under inquiry, may become an investigation, and gains subpoena power only when the Commission issues a formal order.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The stage tells a company what the SEC can demand. Voluntary requests are answered by choice; a subpoena under a formal order must be obeyed. Neither stage is a finding of wrongdoing.
how_it_works: Tips, complaints, referrals and news can open a matter under inquiry (MUI); the bar is low because a MUI only gathers facts (Enforcement Manual 2.2.1).
In a preliminary inquiry no process is issued and no testimony is compelled (17 CFR 202.5(a)); staff ask for documents and interviews voluntarily.
The Commission may issue a formal order of investigation naming staff as officers who can administer oaths, subpoena witnesses and require documents (Manual 2.2.3).
A formal order is an early investigative step, not a determination that anyone violated the law (Manual 2.2.3).
Investigations are nonpublic unless the Commission orders otherwise (202.5(a)).
subtopics.example: Quay Retail's general counsel, Priya, receives an SEC letter asking for sales contracts. They ask whether the company must comply. Outside counsel notes that the letter cites no subpoena, so production is voluntary, but advises cooperating and preserving everything, since the staff can still seek more power from the Commission.

review: Confirm whether each SEC request is voluntary or made under subpoena
Trace every SEC request to a log entry and a response owner
evidence: Copies of SEC letters, subpoenas and any formal order shown
Request log with dates, scope and responses
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel log every SEC request, note its legal basis, and coordinate one company response.
audit_focus.decides: The Commission issues formal orders; counsel decides how the company responds

subtopics.isaca_rule: No formal order, no compulsion: before it, SEC staff can only ask. A formal order lets named staff subpoena documents and testimony, but it is still not a finding of violation.

exam_traps.trap: A formal order of investigation means the SEC has found a violation.
exam_traps.why: The Enforcement Manual calls it an early investigative step that designates officers and grants subpoena power; it decides nothing about guilt.

exam_traps.trap: SEC staff can compel testimony in a matter under inquiry.
exam_traps.why: Compelled testimony needs subpoena power, which comes from a formal order issued in an investigation.

key_terms.definition: The SEC enforcement staff's preliminary look at facts to decide whether a full investigation is worth opening.
A Commission order that names staff as officers with power to subpoena witnesses and documents.
A legal order requiring a person to produce documents or give testimony.

subtopics.memory_aid: Ask first, order second: subpoenas need a formal order.

subtopics.name: The Wells Process
subtopics.definition: The Wells process lets a person whom SEC staff plan to charge learn the proposed charges and answer in writing before the Commission decides.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A Wells notice is the last chance to change the Commission's mind before an action is filed. Treating it as a verdict, or ignoring it, are both costly mistakes.
how_it_works: Rule 5(c) (17 CFR 202.5(c)) lets persons involved in an investigation submit a written statement of their position to the Commission.
A Wells notice says the staff has preliminarily decided to recommend an action, names the proposed violations and invites a submission (Enforcement Manual 2.3).
Absent timing constraints, recipients get four weeks; written submissions are typically capped at 40 pages and videos at 12 minutes (Manual 2.3).
Staff should share salient evidence the recipient may not know; any submission goes to the Commission with the staff's recommendation (Manual 2.3; Rule 5(c)).
Staff may skip the notice when immediate action is needed to protect investors, such as an emergency asset freeze (Manual 2.3).
The Commission may use a submission in any action, and others may be able to obtain it (Manual 2.3).
subtopics.example: Nova Pharma's former sales chief, Jordan, gets a call from SEC staff and then a letter naming proposed charges of misleading investors. Jordan's lawyer drafts a 35-page response arguing the statements were accurate, files it within four weeks, and warns Jordan that the Commission may use it in any later case.

review: Compare the notice's proposed charges with the evidence the staff shared
Confirm the submission deadline, length limit and format
evidence: Written Wells notice and notes of the Wells call
Filed submission with its date and page count
audit_focus.recommend: Have counsel brief the board and file any Wells submission within the stated limits.
audit_focus.decides: The Commission decides whether to bring an action; the board directs the company's response

subtopics.isaca_rule: A Wells notice is a preliminary staff recommendation plus an invitation to respond. Only the Commission decides to sue or start proceedings, and anything submitted can be used against the sender.

exam_traps.trap: A Wells notice is a finding that the recipient broke the law.
exam_traps.why: It reports the staff's preliminary determination to recommend action; the Commission has decided nothing yet.

exam_traps.trap: Everyone the SEC charges first receives a Wells notice.
exam_traps.why: Staff may skip it when urgent action is needed, such as an emergency asset freeze to stop an ongoing fraud.

key_terms.definition: A staff communication saying it preliminarily plans to recommend charges, naming them and inviting a response.
The recipient's written or video statement to the Commission arguing against the proposed action.

subtopics.memory_aid: Wells: warning, evidence shared, written answer, Commission decides.

subtopics.name: Enforcement Outcomes and Settlements
subtopics.definition: SEC enforcement ends in a civil court action, an administrative proceeding, a settlement, a criminal referral or a closed investigation; the SEC itself never prosecutes crimes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Learners must know what an SEC case can and cannot do. Confusing civil SEC remedies with criminal charges brought by the Justice Department is a common trap.
how_it_works: After investigating, the Commission may start administrative proceedings, seek injunctions in court and, for willful violations, refer the matter to the Justice Department (17 CFR 202.5(b)).
The SEC brings civil, not criminal, actions; criminal authorities may run parallel cases (Enforcement Manual 5.2).
A person may offer to settle in writing; the offer waives a hearing and judicial review, and is final only on the Commission's order (17 CFR 201.240).
A settlement resolves only civil or administrative claims; it cannot reach criminal charges, which belong to the Attorney General (202.5(f)).
If staff close a matter, a termination notice is not an exoneration (202.5(d)).
Release No. 33-11417 repealed Rule 202.5(e), the 1972 no-deny settlement policy, from 21 May 2026; the rest of Rule 202.5 stands.
subtopics.example: Cobalt Mining's former operations chief agrees with SEC staff on terms to end an administrative case over misleading reserve estimates. The chief, not their lawyer, signs the written offer, as the rule requires. The division presents it to the Commission, and the deal is final only when the Commission issues its findings and order.

review: Compare settlement terms with the claims and parties they resolve
Confirm the Commission issued a final order accepting the offer
evidence: Executed settlement papers and the order that accepts them
Board minutes approving the company's settlement
audit_focus.recommend: Have counsel confirm in writing that any SEC settlement covers civil claims only, and plan for parallel cases.
audit_focus.decides: The Commission accepts settlements; the Justice Department handles criminal charges

subtopics.isaca_rule: The SEC's tools are civil: court actions, administrative proceedings and settlements. Criminal cases go to the Justice Department, and no SEC settlement can trade away criminal exposure.

exam_traps.trap: The SEC brings criminal charges for willful securities fraud.
exam_traps.why: It refers willful violations to the Department of Justice; the SEC itself brings only civil actions.

exam_traps.trap: A closed SEC investigation clears the company.
exam_traps.why: Rule 5(d) says a termination notice must not be read as exoneration or as a promise that no action will follow.

key_terms.definition: An SEC case heard inside the agency, rather than in federal court, that can lead to sanctions.
A written offer, signed by the person, to resolve an SEC proceeding; final only on the Commission's order.
A civil SEC case and a criminal case on the same facts, run by different authorities.

subtopics.memory_aid: SEC sues civilly; Justice prosecutes; settling ends only the civil side.

subtopics.name: Disclosing an Investigation and Preserving Records
subtopics.definition: Disclosing an SEC investigation is a materiality judgment under the disclosure rules, while preserving related records is a legal duty once proceedings are anticipated.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A company under investigation faces two separate questions: what to tell investors and what to keep. Getting either wrong can add new liability to the original matter.
how_it_works: Regulation S-K Item 103 asks for material pending legal proceedings, including those known to be contemplated by governmental authorities (17 CFR 229.103(a)).
Item 103 turns on materiality, so whether an inquiry must be described is a judgment the company makes with counsel.
SEC staff may send a document preservation letter covering all forms, including messaging apps and personal devices (Enforcement Manual 3.2.2).
A duty to preserve generally arises when litigation is reasonably anticipated or pending (Manual 3.2.2).
Destroying records to obstruct a federal matter, even one only expected, is a crime (18 U.S.C. 1519).
subtopics.example: Ridgeline Software receives an SEC preservation letter about its revenue practices. The legal team issues a hold notice to all sales staff, covering their phone chats, and suspends routine email deletion. Separately, the disclosure committee meets with counsel to judge whether the inquiry is material enough to describe in the next quarterly report.

review: Confirm a legal hold reached every custodian named in the letter
Inspect deletion settings for suspended auto-delete on relevant systems
Evaluate the disclosure committee's materiality analysis
evidence: Legal hold notices with custodian acknowledgments
System logs showing auto-deletion suspended
Disclosure committee minutes on the investigation
audit_focus.recommend: Have the legal team issue holds at once and document the disclosure committee's materiality decision.
audit_focus.decides: Management and the disclosure committee decide disclosure on counsel's advice

subtopics.isaca_rule: Keep everything; decide disclosure on materiality. A preservation duty starts when proceedings are reasonably anticipated, and destroying records to obstruct is a federal crime; whether to disclose an inquiry follows the materiality test in Item 103.

exam_traps.trap: Every SEC inquiry must be disclosed in the next periodic report.
exam_traps.why: Item 103 covers material proceedings, including those known to be contemplated by authorities; whether an inquiry qualifies is a materiality judgment.

exam_traps.trap: Routine deletion schedules can keep running during an investigation.
exam_traps.why: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, relevant records must be kept; staff preservation letters ask for all forms, including messaging apps.

key_terms.definition: An SEC staff letter telling a recipient to keep all potentially relevant documents and messages.
A company instruction suspending deletion of records relevant to a pending or expected proceeding.
The Regulation S-K disclosure item on material pending legal proceedings, including those contemplated by authorities.

subtopics.memory_aid: Keep it all; disclose what is material.

subtopics.name: Common Violations and Enforcement Forums
subtopics.definition: Common violations are the kinds of misconduct the SEC says most often lead to its investigations, such as misleading disclosure, market manipulation, insider trading and unregistered sales.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Naming the violation is the first step in an enforcement question; knowing the forums tells you who hears the case.
how_it_works: The SEC lists six common violations, starting with misleading statements or omissions, price manipulation and theft of customers' funds or securities (How Investigations Work, opened 31 Oct 2026).
The list adds broker-dealers failing to treat customers fairly, insider trading, and selling unregistered securities.
Insider trading is illegal when a person trades while holding material nonpublic information, in breach of a duty to withhold it or not trade (SEC Statutes and Regulations page).
In a civil action, the SEC sues in federal district court for remedies such as an injunction, penalties or disgorgement.
In an administrative proceeding, an administrative law judge independent of the Commission hears the case; either side may appeal to the Commission.
Since SEC v. Jarkesy (2024), defendants facing civil penalties for securities fraud have a jury right, so contested claims of that kind go to federal court.
subtopics.example: Before a product recall is announced, Jordan, a regional sales director at Pinecrest Foods, sells company shares through a relative's account. Market surveillance flags the trade and SEC staff open an inquiry. The compliance officer flags possible insider trading and preserves Jordan's records.

review: Compare preclearance requests with trades by insiders near announcements
Inspect blackout calendars against the dates of material events
evidence: Insider list with dated preclearance approvals
Trading policy acknowledgments signed by insiders
audit_focus.recommend: Have the compliance team test trades by insiders against material event dates each quarter.
audit_focus.decides: SEC staff recommend action, and the Commission votes on it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the violation from the facts: trading on undisclosed material news is insider trading; misleading statements are misrepresentation. The SEC pursues them civilly: contested fraud claims seeking penalties go to federal court (SEC v. Jarkesy, 2024); administrative proceedings remain for other sanctions and settled orders, and many cases settle.

exam_traps.trap: Any profitable trade just before an announcement is market manipulation.
exam_traps.why: Manipulation means trading to move prices artificially. Trading on material nonpublic information in breach of a duty is insider trading, a separate common violation.

exam_traps.trap: An administrative law judge's decision ends the matter.
exam_traps.why: Either side may appeal the initial decision to the Commission, which may affirm, reverse or send it back.

key_terms.definition: Trading or other conduct meant to move a security's price artificially rather than through genuine supply and demand.
A judge independent of the Commission who hears SEC administrative proceedings and issues an initial decision.

subtopics.memory_aid: Name the wrong, then the forum: fraud penalties mean a jury in court.

topics.overview: Title VIII of SOX, the Corporate and Criminal Fraud Accountability Act, made record destruction and securities fraud serious federal crimes, set retention duties for auditors, kept fraud debts alive through bankruptcy and set time limits for investor suits.
can_do: Tell Section 1519's record crime from Section 1520's auditor retention duty
Give the auditor retention periods in the statute and in the SEC rule
Apply the bankruptcy exception and the time limits for securities fraud claims

subtopics.name: Destroying or Falsifying Records
subtopics.definition: Section 802 made it a federal crime for anyone to destroy, alter or falsify records with intent to obstruct a federal matter, punishable by up to 20 years.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It reaches any person, not only auditors or officers, and it can apply before an investigation exists. A cover-up often carries more risk than the original problem.
how_it_works: 18 U.S.C. 1519 covers knowingly altering, destroying, concealing, covering up or falsifying any record, document or tangible object.
The intent must be to impede, obstruct or influence a matter within a federal agency's jurisdiction or a bankruptcy case.
It applies in relation to or in contemplation of such a matter, so no investigation needs to be open yet.
The maximum is 20 years in prison, a fine, or both (18 U.S.C. 1519).
Section 1102 separately punishes corruptly destroying records to impair their use in an official proceeding, also up to 20 years (18 U.S.C. 1512(c)).
subtopics.example: A plant manager at Fernway Chemicals expects a federal environmental inspection next month. Fearing fines, they edit the plant's emissions log to remove three spills. A compliance analyst finds the original file on a backup and reports it to counsel, who explains that editing records in anticipation of a federal inspection can be a crime.

review: Compare edited records with backups and system audit trails
Inspect change logs for edits made once a federal matter was expected
evidence: System audit trail showing who changed each record and when
Preserved snapshots taken before any suspected change
audit_focus.recommend: Have management lock records relevant to any expected federal review and report suspected tampering to counsel at once.
audit_focus.decides: Prosecutors decide charges; the board oversees the company's response

subtopics.isaca_rule: Anyone, any record, intent to obstruct, a federal matter pending or expected: that is Section 1519, up to 20 years. It is wider than the auditor workpaper duty in Section 1520.

exam_traps.trap: Destroying records is a crime only once an investigation has started.
exam_traps.why: Section 1519 also covers acts in contemplation of a federal matter, so destruction before any inquiry can qualify.

exam_traps.trap: Section 802's record crimes apply only to auditors.
exam_traps.why: Section 1519 applies to whoever alters or destroys records; only Section 1520 is aimed at accountants who audit issuers.

key_terms.definition: Acting to impede or influence an investigation or proceeding, for example by destroying or falsifying evidence.
Done while expecting a future matter, before it formally begins.

subtopics.memory_aid: 1519: anyone, any record, any federal matter, even one only expected.

subtopics.name: Audit Workpaper Retention
subtopics.definition: Audit workpaper retention is the duty of an issuer's auditor to keep audit and review records for a set period: five years by statute, seven by SEC rule.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These records are how regulators and courts test an audit later. Two numbers sit in two sources, and the exam asks which one auditors must meet.
how_it_works: 18 U.S.C. 1520 (Section 802) has issuer auditors keep workpapers five years from the end of the fiscal period in which the audit or review was concluded.
Knowingly and willfully breaking that duty, or the SEC's retention rules, carries up to 10 years in prison (1520(b)).
The SEC's Rule 2-06 (17 CFR 210.2-06) requires seven years after the auditor concludes the audit or review.
Rule 2-06 covers workpapers, memos, correspondence and electronic records holding conclusions, opinions, analysis or financial data.
It also covers records that conflict with the auditor's final conclusions on a significant matter, such as consultations on differences of opinion.

rows.label: Who
cells: Auditors of issuers and registered investment companies

rows.label: Period
cells: Five years from the end of the fiscal period in which the audit or review ended
Seven years after the audit or review ends
Six or three years, by record type

rows.label: Records
cells: Workpapers plus memos, correspondence and conflicting views

subtopics.example: At a regional accounting practice, an IT lead plans to purge client folders after five years to save storage. The quality partner stops the change: the SEC's rule runs longer, and it also reaches emails and memos recording disagreements with the final conclusions, which the purge would have deleted first.

review: Compare the retention schedule with Rule 2-06's seven-year period
Check closed engagements to confirm their records still exist
Inspect deletion jobs for exceptions covering engagement records

Archived engagement files with closing dates

subtopics.isaca_rule: For an issuer's auditor, meet the longer period: seven years under Rule 2-06, which also reaches memos, correspondence and dissenting views. The five years in 18 U.S.C. 1520 is the statute's own floor.

exam_traps.trap: Auditors only need to keep workpapers for five years.
exam_traps.why: Five years is the statute (18 U.S.C. 1520); the SEC's Rule 2-06 requires seven years after the audit or review is concluded.

exam_traps.trap: Rule 17a-4 is the SOX retention rule for auditors.
exam_traps.why: Rule 17a-4 covers the records of exchange members, brokers and dealers; auditors' issuer records fall under Rule 2-06.

key_terms.definition: An auditor's record of procedures applied, evidence obtained and conclusions reached (Rule 2-06(b)).
An engagement on financial statements narrower than an audit; Rule 2-06 covers its records as well.
