subtopics.name: Bankruptcy, Time Limits and Securities Fraud
subtopics.definition: Sections 803, 804 and 807 made securities fraud debts survive bankruptcy, set time limits for private fraud suits, and created a 25-year securities fraud crime.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Together they make fraud costly and lasting for wrongdoers and give investors a clear window to sue. Each section carries one number the exam can test.
how_it_works: Section 803 added 11 U.S.C. 523(a)(19): debts for securities law violations or securities fraud are not discharged in bankruptcy.
That covers debts from judgments, orders, settlement agreements the debtor signed, and orders for damages, fines, penalties or disgorgement.
Section 804 (28 U.S.C. 1658(b)): private securities fraud claims must be filed within two years of discovery or five years of the violation, whichever comes first.
Section 804 created no new right to sue; it set time limits for existing private claims.
Section 807 created 18 U.S.C. 1348: knowingly executing a scheme to defraud in connection with a reporting company's securities carries up to 25 years.
subtopics.example: Investors in Larkspur Energy learn in 2026 that its reserve reports were inflated. Their lawyer checks the dates: the misleading reports came out in 2024, so the suit fits inside both the two-year limit from discovery and the five-year limit from the violation, and the lawyer files promptly.

review: Compare claim dates with the two-year and five-year limits
Trace any settlement debts to the agreements that created them
evidence: Chronology showing when misstatements were made and found
Settlement agreements and court orders showing amounts owed
audit_focus.recommend: Have counsel calendar limitation dates for any investor claims and record settlement debts accurately.
audit_focus.decides: Courts decide limits and discharge; counsel advises the board on claims

subtopics.isaca_rule: Securities fraud debts survive bankruptcy, even from a settlement (803). Private fraud suits: two years from discovery or five from the violation, whichever is first (804). Securities fraud itself: up to 25 years (807).

exam_traps.trap: A settlement that admits no wrongdoing can be wiped out in bankruptcy.
exam_traps.why: Section 523(a)(19) covers any settlement agreement the debtor entered into, without asking about admissions.

exam_traps.trap: Investors always have five years to sue for securities fraud.
exam_traps.why: The claim must be brought by the earlier of two years after discovery or five years after the violation.

key_terms.definition: A debt that survives bankruptcy and must still be paid after the case ends.
The deadline for bringing a legal claim, after which the claim is barred.
An order to give up profits gained from a violation.

subtopics.memory_aid: 803 survives, 804 two-or-five, 807 twenty-five.

topics.overview: Federal law protects and rewards people who report securities fraud. SOX Section 806 shields employees from retaliation through a Labor Department process; Dodd-Frank added SEC cash awards and a direct court route; and SOX Section 1107 makes retaliating against informants a crime.
can_do: Name who Section 806 protects, where the complaint goes and by when
Apply the Dodd-Frank award conditions and exclusions
Match a retaliation fact pattern to Section 806, Section 21F(h) or Section 1107

subtopics.name: Section 806 Retaliation Protection
subtopics.definition: Section 806 protects employees of public companies from retaliation for reporting suspected fraud or securities violations, starting with a complaint to the Secretary of Labor.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Employees often spot fraud first. Without protection few would report; with it, a company that punishes a good-faith report faces reinstatement, back pay and damages.
how_it_works: Covered: companies registered under Exchange Act Section 12 or reporting under 15(d), their consolidated subsidiaries and affiliates, and rating organizations (18 U.S.C. 1514A(a)).
Protected: giving information on mail, wire, bank or securities fraud, SEC rule violations or shareholder fraud to a federal agency, Congress or a supervisor.
Also protected: filing, testifying in or assisting a related proceeding (1514A(a)(2)).
The employee files with the Secretary of Labor within 180 days of the violation or of learning of it (1514A(b)(2)(D)).
With no final Labor decision in 180 days, and no bad-faith delay by the employee, they may sue in federal court with a jury (1514A(b)).
Remedies: reinstatement with seniority, back pay with interest, and special damages including litigation costs and attorney fees (1514A(c)).
subtopics.example: Theo, a payroll specialist at a listed retailer's consolidated subsidiary, tells the regional controller that bonuses are being booked to the wrong year to beat analyst targets. Two weeks later Theo is moved to a night shift with lower pay. Theo files a complaint with the Department of Labor, naming both the subsidiary and the parent.

review: Trace each reported concern to its intake record and outcome
Compare later job actions against reporters with peers' treatment
evidence: Hotline and complaint logs with dates and resolutions
HR records of transfers, pay changes and terminations after reports
audit_focus.recommend: Have the audit committee review any adverse action against an employee who reported fraud before it takes effect.
audit_focus.decides: The Labor Department, then a federal court, decides retaliation claims

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 806 protects public company employees, including those of consolidated subsidiaries, who report fraud internally or to authorities. Complaint to the Secretary of Labor within 180 days; court with a jury if Labor has not decided within 180 days.

exam_traps.trap: Only reports made to the SEC are protected under Section 806.
exam_traps.why: Reports to a supervisor or another person with authority to investigate, to Congress or to a federal agency are all protected.

exam_traps.trap: Section 806 complaints go straight to federal court.
exam_traps.why: The employee first files with the Secretary of Labor; court is open only if Labor has not decided within 180 days.

key_terms.definition: Firing, demoting, suspending, threatening, harassing or otherwise discriminating against an employee for a protected act.
A lawful report or assistance about suspected fraud or securities violations that the law shields from retaliation.

subtopics.memory_aid: 806: report, protected; Labor first, 180 days.

subtopics.name: SEC Whistleblower Awards
subtopics.definition: Dodd-Frank Section 922 created SEC awards of 10 to 30 percent of collected sanctions for people who voluntarily give original information leading to actions over $1 million.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Money brings tips the SEC might never get otherwise. Knowing who qualifies, and who is excluded, is central to whistleblower questions.
how_it_works: A covered action is an SEC judicial or administrative action with monetary sanctions over $1 million (15 U.S.C. 78u-6(a)(1)).
Original information comes from the whistleblower's own knowledge or analysis and is not already known to the SEC from another source (78u-6(a)(3)).
Awards total 10 to 30 percent of sanctions collected, set at the SEC's discretion, and are paid from its Investor Protection Fund (78u-6(b)).
No award goes to regulators' or law enforcement staff, people convicted in the matter, or auditors whose required-audit tip is contrary to Section 10A (78u-6(c)(2)).
Anonymous claimants must use a lawyer, and the SEC must keep identifying information confidential (78u-6(d), (h)(2)).
After the SEC posts a notice of covered action, claimants have 90 calendar days to apply (SEC Whistleblower Program page).
subtopics.example: Rosa, a sales engineer at a medical device maker, sees invoices backdated to inflate revenue. Rosa sends documents and their own analysis to the SEC through a lawyer, without giving a name. Two years later the SEC collects $6 million in sanctions and posts a notice of covered action, and the lawyer files Rosa's claim in time.

review: Compare the company's speak-up policy with SEC whistleblower protections
Inspect employment agreements for clauses that discourage contacting the SEC
evidence: Employment and severance agreement templates reviewed by counsel
Speak-up policy and training completion records
audit_focus.recommend: Have legal counsel remove any agreement language that could stop employees from reporting to the SEC.
audit_focus.decides: SEC staff process claims; the Commission decides awards and amounts

subtopics.isaca_rule: Dodd-Frank awards: original information, given voluntarily to the SEC, leading to sanctions over $1 million; 10 to 30 percent of what is collected, paid from the SEC's fund. Check the exclusions, including auditors acting contrary to Section 10A.

exam_traps.trap: The company that committed the fraud pays the whistleblower's award.
exam_traps.why: Awards are paid from the SEC's Investor Protection Fund; the wrongdoer pays sanctions to the government.

exam_traps.trap: A whistleblower must report inside the company before an award is possible.
exam_traps.why: Section 21F does not list internal reporting as an award condition; the information must reach the SEC in the form it requires.

key_terms.definition: Information from a whistleblower's own knowledge or analysis that the SEC does not already have from another source.
An SEC court or administrative action that results in monetary sanctions over $1 million.

subtopics.memory_aid: Original, voluntary, over a million: 10 to 30 percent from the SEC's fund.

subtopics.name: Other Anti-Retaliation Routes
subtopics.definition: Beyond Section 806, Dodd-Frank lets SEC whistleblowers sue retaliating employers directly in court, and SOX Section 1107 makes retaliating against informants a federal crime.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Each route has its own forum, deadline and remedy. Exam items test which route a fact pattern points to, and whether the consequence is civil or criminal.
how_it_works: Section 21F(h) bars retaliation for giving the SEC information, assisting its actions, or making disclosures SOX requires or protects (15 U.S.C. 78u-6(h)(1)(A)).
Protection covers only people who reported to the SEC in writing before the retaliation (17 CFR 240.21F-2(d)(1)).
The employee sues directly in federal district court; no Labor complaint comes first (78u-6(h)(1)(B)(i)).
Deadline: six years after the violation or three years after the material facts were known, and never more than 10 years (78u-6(h)(1)(B)(iii)).
Relief: reinstatement, two times back pay with interest, and litigation costs and attorney fees (78u-6(h)(1)(C)).
Section 1107 (18 U.S.C. 1513(e)): knowingly retaliating against anyone for giving law enforcement truthful information about a federal offense carries up to 10 years in prison.

rows.label: Starts with
cells: Complaint to the Secretary of Labor

rows.label: Deadline
cells: 6 years, or 3 from knowledge; 10 at most

rows.label: Pay relief
cells: Two times back pay with interest

subtopics.example: Ivy, a fund analyst, gives the SEC evidence of hidden fees and also speaks to FBI agents. Soon after, Ivy is demoted. Ivy's lawyer skips the Labor process and sues in federal court under Section 21F, seeking double back pay, while prosecutors consider whether the demotion, as payback for talking to the FBI, is a crime.

review: Map each reporting channel to the protection and forum it triggers
Inspect adverse actions taken soon after an employee reported externally
evidence: Legal analysis of reports made to the SEC and law enforcement
HR action log with dates and decision makers
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel review adverse actions against known reporters before they take effect.
audit_focus.decides: Courts decide civil claims; prosecutors decide criminal charges with the board kept informed

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the route to the facts: Section 806 starts with Labor within 180 days; Dodd-Frank 21F(h) goes straight to court with double back pay; Section 1107 is a crime, up to 10 years, for retaliating against informants to law enforcement.

exam_traps.trap: Retaliating against an informant can only lead to civil remedies.
exam_traps.why: Section 1107 makes knowing retaliation against a person who gave law enforcement truthful information a crime, with up to 10 years.

exam_traps.trap: Dodd-Frank retaliation claims must start at the Department of Labor.
exam_traps.why: Section 21F(h) lets the individual sue directly in federal district court.

key_terms.definition: Relief under Dodd-Frank of two times the back pay owed, with interest.
A person who gives law enforcement truthful information about a possible federal offense.

subtopics.memory_aid: Labor in 180 days, court direct, crime for revenge.

subtopics.name: Whistleblowers Outside the United States
subtopics.definition: Foreign whistleblowers are people outside the United States who report securities violations to the SEC; award eligibility turns on who employs them, not on citizenship.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Issuers have staff and subsidiaries abroad; testing nationality instead of employer gives wrong answers about who may claim an award.
how_it_works: A whistleblower is any individual who gives the SEC information on a securities law violation as the SEC requires (15 U.S.C. 78u-6(a)(6), opened 31 Oct 2026).
Neither that definition nor the award exclusions in Rule 21F-8(c) sets a citizenship or residence test.
The statute bars awards to staff of appropriate regulatory agencies, the Justice Department, SROs, the PCAOB and any law enforcement organization; it names no foreign regulator (78u-6(c)(2)(A)).
Rule 21F-8(c)(2) adds anyone working for a foreign government or a foreign financial regulatory authority, now or when they got the information (17 CFR 240.21F-8).
The SEC may share whistleblower information with foreign securities and law enforcement authorities under confidentiality assurances it sets (78u-6(h)(2)(D)).
subtopics.example: Ana, a sales manager at the Brazilian subsidiary of a U.S.-listed issuer, asks a lawyer whether a written SEC tip about bribes could earn an award, though they are not a U.S. citizen. The lawyer says citizenship is not a test, but a friend who examines banks for Brazil's regulator would be excluded.

review: Compare each translated whistleblower policy with the English version
Inspect hotline intake records from foreign subsidiaries
evidence: Translated policies with dated approvals
Training attendance records for staff abroad
audit_focus.recommend: Have the compliance team describe the SEC reporting route accurately in every language version of the policy.
audit_focus.decides: SEC staff review award claims, and the Commission decides them

subtopics.isaca_rule: For award eligibility abroad, ask who employed the tipster when they learned the facts. Citizenship and residence are not tests; Rule 21F-8(c)(2) excludes staff of foreign governments and foreign financial regulators, on top of the statute's list.

exam_traps.trap: Only U.S. citizens or residents can receive SEC whistleblower awards.
exam_traps.why: The statute defines a whistleblower as any individual who reports to the SEC; the exclusions turn on employer and conduct, not nationality.

exam_traps.trap: The statute's exclusions name no foreign regulator, so foreign regulators' staff qualify.
exam_traps.why: Rule 21F-8(c)(2) extends the bar to members, officers and employees of foreign governments and foreign financial regulatory authorities.

key_terms.definition: A foreign securities authority or other foreign government body that regulates financial activities (Exchange Act Section 3(a)(52)).
The SEC form for a tip, complaint or referral that a person uses to seek award eligibility.

subtopics.memory_aid: Ask who employs them, not where they live.

topics.overview: Title IX of SOX, the White-Collar Crime Penalty Enhancement Act of 2002, raised maximum penalties for fraud, made attempts and conspiracies as punishable as the finished crime, and told the Sentencing Commission to toughen its guidelines. Section 906, also in Title IX, is taught with the officer certifications in Domain 3.
can_do: Apply the same-penalty rule to attempts and conspiracies
Give the before-and-after maximums for mail and wire fraud
Tell Title IX's numbers from securities fraud's 25 years under Section 807

subtopics.name: Attempts and Conspiracies
subtopics.definition: Section 902 makes attempting or conspiring to commit a federal fraud offense punishable by the same penalties as the completed offense.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Fraud schemes are often caught before they finish. This rule means an interrupted or failed plan carries the same statutory maximum as a successful one.
how_it_works: Section 902 added 18 U.S.C. 1349 to chapter 63 of title 18, the chapter on mail fraud and other frauds.
Chapter 63 holds offenses such as mail fraud (1341), wire fraud (1343) and securities fraud (1348).
Anyone who attempts or conspires to commit such an offense faces the same penalties as the offense that was the object.
No completed trade, loss or victim is needed for an attempt or conspiracy charge.
subtopics.example: A trader at Pinecrest Brokerage starts entering fake customer orders to push up a thinly traded stock, but the firm's surveillance team blocks them before any order executes. The firm's counsel explains that an attempt to commit securities fraud is punished like the finished offense, and the firm reports the conduct.

review: Inspect surveillance alerts for schemes stopped before completion
Trace escalation of blocked schemes to compliance and counsel
evidence: Surveillance alert records showing blocked orders or transfers
Escalation memos to counsel with dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have compliance escalate attempted schemes to counsel even when no loss occurred.
audit_focus.decides: Prosecutors decide whether to charge an attempt or conspiracy; the board oversees reporting

subtopics.isaca_rule: Under Section 902, an attempt or conspiracy equals the offense for penalty purposes. A scheme stopped before anyone loses money still carries the full statutory maximum.

exam_traps.trap: An unfinished fraud scheme carries a lower statutory maximum.
exam_traps.why: 18 U.S.C. 1349 gives attempts and conspiracies the same penalties as the offense they aimed at.

exam_traps.trap: No crime occurs if no investor lost money.
exam_traps.why: Attempting or conspiring to commit a chapter 63 fraud offense is a crime in itself.

key_terms.definition: An agreement between two or more people to commit a crime.
An effort to commit a crime that falls short of completion.

subtopics.memory_aid: Tried or planned it? Same maximum as doing it.

subtopics.name: Higher Fraud and Pension Penalties
subtopics.definition: Sections 903 to 905 raised maximum penalties for mail and wire fraud and for willful pension reporting violations, and directed tougher sentencing guidelines.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Congress raised these penalties to deter white-collar fraud. Exam items test the before-and-after numbers and which offense each number belongs to.
how_it_works: Section 903 raised the maximum prison term for mail fraud (18 U.S.C. 1341) and wire fraud (1343) from five to 20 years.
A higher tier, up to 30 years and a $1 million fine, applies when the fraud affects a financial institution or a declared disaster (18 U.S.C. 1341, 1343).
Section 904 raised willful ERISA reporting penalties to $100,000 (from $5,000) and 10 years (from one) for individuals, and $500,000 for entities (29 U.S.C. 1131).
Section 905 told the U.S. Sentencing Commission to review its guidelines so they reflect the Act's higher penalties.
Section 805 did the same for obstruction and extensive fraud, including offenses under Sections 1519 and 1520.
subtopics.example: A union pension plan's administrator willfully skips a required financial report to hide investment losses. Prosecutors note that, since 2002, a willful ERISA reporting violation can bring up to 10 years in prison and a $100,000 fine for an individual, not the old one year and $5,000.

review: Compare training materials' penalty figures with the current U.S. Code
Confirm pension plan reports were filed on time
evidence: Training slides with penalty figures and their sources
Plan filing records with submission dates
audit_focus.recommend: Have the compliance team update penalty figures in training each year from the current U.S. Code.
audit_focus.decides: Judges set sentences; plan administrators must file the reports

subtopics.isaca_rule: Title IX numbers: mail and wire fraud went from 5 to 20 years (903); willful ERISA reporting violations reach $100,000 and 10 years for individuals and $500,000 for entities (904). Securities fraud's 25 years comes from Section 807.

exam_traps.trap: SOX set mail fraud's maximum at 25 years.
exam_traps.why: Section 903 set 20 years; 25 years is the maximum for securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. 1348, created by Section 807.

exam_traps.trap: Title IX contains the whistleblower protections.
exam_traps.why: Whistleblower protection is Section 806 in Title VIII; Title IX raised white-collar penalties and added the Section 906 certification.

key_terms.definition: The Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974, which governs private pension and benefit plans.
Federal rules courts consult to set a sentence within the statutory maximum.

subtopics.memory_aid: Title IX: five became 20 for mail and wire.

topics.overview: The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 set out to promote financial stability, end too big to fail and bailouts, and protect consumers. It created a council to watch system-wide risk, a process to liquidate failing financial companies, a Federal Insurance Office, and limits on banks' own trading.
can_do: State Dodd-Frank's aims from its own long title
Tell the FSOC's role from the Federal Insurance Office's
Explain who bears losses under orderly liquidation
Describe what the Volcker Rule bars and permits

subtopics.name: Dodd-Frank's Purposes and the FSOC
subtopics.definition: The Dodd-Frank Act, signed on 21 July 2010, reformed U.S. financial regulation and created the Financial Stability Oversight Council to watch for threats to stability.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Dodd-Frank is the second major reform after SOX, and it amended SOX. Knowing its stated aims and new bodies places each provision in context.
how_it_works: Its long title lists the aims: promote financial stability through accountability and transparency, end 'too big to fail', end bailouts to protect taxpayers, and protect consumers (Pub. L. 111-203).
Title I created the Financial Stability Oversight Council (FSOC), chaired by the Treasury Secretary, with 10 voting members (Section 111(b)).
Voting members include the heads of the Federal Reserve Board, the SEC, the FDIC and the CFTC, plus an independent member with insurance expertise.
The FSOC identifies risks to U.S. financial stability, promotes market discipline and responds to emerging threats (Section 112(a)(1)).
It can require Federal Reserve supervision of nonbank financial companies whose distress or activities could threaten stability (Section 112(a)(2)(H)).
subtopics.example: Ledgerline, a fast-growing payments company, is not a bank. Its general counsel warns the board that if Ledgerline's distress could threaten U.S. financial stability, the FSOC can place it under Federal Reserve supervision, with stricter standards. The board asks finance to model the company's links to other large firms.

review: Map Dodd-Frank titles to the company's business lines
Evaluate whether the company could draw an FSOC designation
evidence: Regulatory inventory of the Dodd-Frank provisions that apply
Board materials on system-wide risk exposure
audit_focus.recommend: Have the general counsel keep a current map of the Dodd-Frank provisions that apply to the company.
audit_focus.decides: The Council decides designations; the board oversees the company's response

subtopics.isaca_rule: Dodd-Frank (Pub. L. 111-203, 21 July 2010) aims at financial stability, an end to too big to fail and bailouts, and consumer protection. Its Title I council, the FSOC, chaired by the Treasury Secretary, watches system-wide risk.

exam_traps.trap: Dodd-Frank replaced the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
exam_traps.why: It amended SOX in places, such as Section 404(c) and the whistleblower rules, but SOX remains in force.

exam_traps.trap: The SEC chair leads the FSOC.
exam_traps.why: The Treasury Secretary chairs the Council; the SEC chair is one of its voting members (Section 111(b)).

key_terms.definition: The Dodd-Frank council, chaired by the Treasury Secretary, that monitors and responds to risks to U.S. financial stability.
A financial firm that is not a bank holding company, which the FSOC can place under Federal Reserve supervision.
Investors and creditors limiting risk-taking because they expect no government rescue.

subtopics.memory_aid: Treasury chairs the FSOC; stability is its job.

subtopics.name: Orderly Liquidation Authority
subtopics.definition: Title II's orderly liquidation authority lets the FDIC act as receiver to wind down a failing financial company that threatens stability, without taxpayer losses.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It turns the Act's promise to end bailouts into a process: failing firms are liquidated, not rescued, and losses fall on those who invested in them.
how_it_works: Purpose: liquidate failing financial companies that pose significant risk to U.S. financial stability, mitigating that risk and minimizing moral hazard (Section 204(a)).
Creditors and shareholders bear the losses, and management responsible for the failure is not retained (Section 204(a)(1)-(2)).
The FDIC acts as receiver once appointed (Section 204(b)).
Every company put into receivership must be liquidated, and no taxpayer funds may be used to prevent liquidation (Section 214(a)).
Costs are recovered from the company's assets or through assessments on the financial sector; taxpayers bear no losses (Section 214(b)-(c)).
subtopics.example: Regulators begin winding down Halsey Capital, a large financial group whose collapse could disrupt funding markets. The FDIC, as receiver, replaces the executives responsible, sells business lines and leaves shareholders with nothing. Bondholders recover only part of their claims, and the remaining costs are billed to large financial firms through assessments.

review: Evaluate how disclosures describe who absorbs losses in a failure
Compare investor materials with Title II's order of losses
evidence: Risk factor disclosures on failure and liquidation
Board materials on failure scenarios
audit_focus.recommend: Have management state plainly in disclosures that shareholders and creditors, not taxpayers, would absorb losses in a liquidation.
audit_focus.decides: The FDIC as receiver runs the wind-down; the board cooperates

subtopics.isaca_rule: Orderly liquidation means liquidation, never rescue: the FDIC as receiver, losses on shareholders and creditors, responsible managers out, costs recovered from assets or industry assessments, and no losses for taxpayers.

exam_traps.trap: Taxpayers fund the liquidation and are repaid later.
exam_traps.why: Section 214 bars taxpayer funds that prevent liquidation and says taxpayers bear no losses; costs come from assets or industry assessments.

exam_traps.trap: Managers stay on to run the company through the process.
exam_traps.why: Section 204(a)(2) says management responsible for the company's condition will not be retained.

key_terms.definition: The party appointed to take control of a failed company and wind it down; under Title II, the FDIC.
Taking on more risk because someone else is expected to bear the losses.

subtopics.memory_aid: Liquidate, don't rescue: owners and lenders lose, taxpayers don't.

subtopics.name: The Federal Insurance Office and the Volcker Rule
subtopics.definition: Dodd-Frank created a Federal Insurance Office in the Treasury to monitor insurance, and Section 619, called the Volcker Rule, limits banking entities' proprietary trading and fund stakes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Both appear in the course's Dodd-Frank list. The exam tests what each does and does not do, such as regulating insurers directly or banning all bank trading.
how_it_works: Section 502 created the Federal Insurance Office within the Treasury, headed by a Director the Treasury Secretary appoints (31 U.S.C. 313(a)-(b)).
The Office monitors the insurance industry, including gaps that could feed a systemic crisis, advises the Secretary, and may recommend that the FSOC designate an insurer (313(c)).
It has no general supervisory or regulatory authority over the business of insurance (313(k)), and its Director is a nonvoting FSOC member.
Section 619 bars banking entities from proprietary trading and from owning or sponsoring hedge funds or private equity funds, unless an exception applies.
Permitted: government obligations, market making sized to client demand, risk-reducing hedges (Bank Holding Company Act Section 13(d)(1), added by Section 619; 12 U.S.C. 1851(d)(1)).
subtopics.example: Westbrook Bank's trading desk wants to buy corporate bonds purely to profit from short-term price moves. Compliance blocks the trade as proprietary trading under Section 619. The desk may still make markets in those bonds sized to expected client demand, and may hedge specific risks in positions it already holds.

review: Check trading desk positions and match each to a permitted activity
Compare desk inventory limits with expected client demand
evidence: Desk mandates naming the permitted activity relied on
Inventory and hedging records by desk
audit_focus.recommend: Have the bank's compliance team document the permitted activity for every trading desk.
audit_focus.decides: Senior management approves desk mandates within the agencies' rules

subtopics.isaca_rule: The Federal Insurance Office monitors and advises but does not regulate insurers. Section 619 bars banking entities from proprietary trading and hedge or private equity fund stakes, except listed permitted activities such as market making and hedging.

exam_traps.trap: The Federal Insurance Office regulates and supervises insurance companies.
exam_traps.why: 31 U.S.C. 313(k) says it has no general supervisory or regulatory authority over the business of insurance.

exam_traps.trap: The Volcker Rule bans all trading by banks.
exam_traps.why: Section 619 permits activities such as market making, underwriting, hedging and trading government obligations.

key_terms.definition: A banking entity trading for its own account to profit, rather than for customers.
Standing ready to buy and sell a security for clients, sized to their reasonably expected near-term demand.

subtopics.memory_aid: FIO watches insurance; Volcker stops banks betting their own money.

topics.overview: Dodd-Frank widened the PCAOB's reach to the auditors of brokers and dealers and let the Board share confidential information with foreign auditor regulators. The Basel bank capital standards are held from these notes until a primary source can be checked.
can_do: Explain how Dodd-Frank extended PCAOB oversight to auditors of brokers and dealers
Tell the PCAOB's role over auditors from the SEC's role over broker-dealers
List the conditions for PCAOB sharing with foreign auditor regulators

subtopics.name: PCAOB Oversight of Broker and Dealer Auditors
subtopics.definition: Dodd-Frank Section 982 extended the PCAOB's oversight from the auditors of public companies to the auditors of brokers and dealers that file certified financial statements.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Customers with assets at brokers and dealers rely on their audited statements. The change put those audits under the independent oversight SOX created for issuer audits.
how_it_works: Section 982 replaced 'issuers' with 'issuers, brokers, and dealers' across the PCAOB's mission in SOX Section 101.
Firms that prepare audit reports for brokers or dealers register with the Board, unless exempt from its inspection program (SOX Sections 102 and 104(a)(2)(D)).
The Board may, by rule, inspect firms that audit brokers or dealers; such rules need prior SEC approval (SOX Section 104(a)(2)).
The Board's support fees are allocated among brokers and dealers in proportion to their net capital (SOX Section 109(h)).
The PCAOB still oversees the audit firm; brokers and dealers themselves are regulated by the SEC and self-regulatory organizations.
subtopics.example: Calder Securities, a small broker-dealer, hires a local CPA practice to audit its annual statements. The partner learns the practice must register with the Board and follow its standards for this engagement, and that its work may be inspected. Calder itself stays under the SEC and FINRA.

review: Confirm the broker-dealer's audit firm is registered with the PCAOB
Inspect the audit report for reference to PCAOB standards
evidence: Public PCAOB listing showing the firm's registration status
Signed audit report filed with the annual statements
audit_focus.recommend: Have the broker-dealer's management confirm its audit firm's PCAOB registration before each engagement.
audit_focus.decides: The audit firm answers to the Board; management chooses a registered firm

subtopics.isaca_rule: Since Dodd-Frank, the PCAOB oversees auditors of issuers, brokers and dealers: registration, standards, inspections and discipline. It regulates the auditor, never the broker-dealer, and its inspection rules need SEC approval.

exam_traps.trap: Dodd-Frank abolished the PCAOB.
exam_traps.why: It widened the PCAOB's reach to auditors of brokers and dealers; the Board continues under SEC oversight.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB now inspects broker-dealers themselves.
exam_traps.why: It inspects audit firms; brokers and dealers are regulated by the SEC and self-regulatory organizations.

key_terms.definition: A firm registered with the SEC to trade securities for customers, for itself, or both.
A broker-dealer's capital measure, which the PCAOB uses to share its support fees among brokers and dealers.

subtopics.memory_aid: 982: auditors of brokers and dealers join the PCAOB's watch.

subtopics.name: Sharing Information with Foreign Auditor Regulators
subtopics.definition: Dodd-Frank Section 981 lets the PCAOB share confidential inspection and investigation information with foreign auditor oversight authorities when set conditions are met.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Many audit firms work across borders. Sharing lets regulators coordinate oversight of the same firms while keeping sensitive information protected.
how_it_works: Section 981 defines a foreign auditor oversight authority: a body a foreign government empowers to inspect or regulate public accounting firms.
The PCAOB may share information, which stays confidential and privileged in its hands, at the Board's discretion (SOX Section 105(b)(5)(C)).
The Board must find sharing necessary to accomplish the Act's purposes or to protect investors.
The foreign authority must give confidentiality assurances and describe its information systems and controls and its relevant laws.
The Board must also determine that sharing is appropriate.
subtopics.example: A PCAOB inspection team reviews the U.S. work of an audit firm that a regulator abroad also oversees. The foreign regulator asks for the findings. Before sharing, the Board obtains written confidentiality assurances, a description of the regulator's information controls and access laws, and records why sharing protects investors.

review: Confirm each sharing request met the statutory conditions
Trace shared files to the confidentiality assurances received
evidence: Signed letters from the foreign body on keeping data secret
Board determination recording why sharing was appropriate
audit_focus.recommend: Have PCAOB staff document every statutory condition before releasing information to a foreign authority.
audit_focus.decides: The Board itself makes the final call on each request

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 981 permits, but never requires, PCAOB sharing with foreign auditor regulators. Three gates: necessity for the Act's purposes or investor protection, the foreign body's assurances and descriptions, and a Board finding that sharing is appropriate.

exam_traps.trap: Shared PCAOB information loses its confidential status.
exam_traps.why: Section 981 says the information keeps its confidential and privileged status in the Board's hands.

exam_traps.trap: The PCAOB must share whenever a foreign regulator asks.
exam_traps.why: Sharing is at the Board's discretion and only after the statutory conditions are met.

key_terms.definition: A body a foreign government empowers to inspect or regulate public accounting firms.
Information protected from forced disclosure in legal proceedings.

subtopics.memory_aid: Share with care: need, assurances, the Board's yes.

topics.overview: Dodd-Frank changed SOX in three ways learners meet often: it exempted smaller filers from the auditor's internal control attestation, strengthened the Section 806 whistleblower rules, and required listed companies to claw back pay awarded on numbers later restated.
can_do: State exactly what Section 404(c) exempts, and for whom
Compare the 2002 and current versions of Section 806
Tell a Rule 10D-1 clawback from a Section 304 forfeiture

subtopics.name: Section 404(c) and the Smaller-Issuer Study
subtopics.definition: Dodd-Frank Section 989G(a) added Section 404(c), which exempts issuers that are neither large accelerated nor accelerated filers from the auditor's internal control attestation.
subtopics.why_it_matters: It is why many smaller companies get no auditor opinion on internal control. The exam tests exactly what was exempted, and what was not.
how_it_works: Section 404(c) says Section 404(b) does not apply to an issuer that is neither a large accelerated filer nor an accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2.
Section 404(a) still applies: management must report on and assess internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) as of year-end.
Section 989G(b) ordered an SEC study, due within nine months, on easing 404(b) for issuers with market capitalization between $75 million and $250 million.
The study was not an exemption; the exemption rests on filer status, which Rule 12b-2 defines.
The JOBS Act later exempted emerging growth companies from 404(b) as well (15 U.S.C. 7262(b)).
subtopics.example: Beacon Tools has always filed as a smaller company with no outside opinion on its controls. After its status changes to accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2, its CFO learns the old exemption no longer fits: the next annual report needs the outside firm's internal control report as well as management's own.

review: Reperform the year-end filer status determination with the finance team
Compare the 10-K's control reports with the filer status reached
evidence: Year-end filer status worksheet and its inputs
Signed outside firm attestation report, when one is required
audit_focus.recommend: Have the CFO confirm filer status each year and plan for an outside attestation when status changes.
audit_focus.decides: Management assesses ICFR; the audit committee oversees the outside firm

subtopics.isaca_rule: Section 404(c) removes only 404(b), the auditor's attestation, and only for issuers that are neither large accelerated nor accelerated filers. Management's 404(a) assessment still applies. The $75 million to $250 million range in 989G(b) was a study, not a rule.

exam_traps.trap: Dodd-Frank exempted small companies from all of Section 404.
exam_traps.why: Section 404(c) removes only the auditor's attestation under 404(b); management's assessment under 404(a) remains.

exam_traps.trap: Companies under $250 million in market value are exempt from 404(b).
exam_traps.why: $75 million to $250 million was the range for an SEC study under 989G(b); the exemption turns on Rule 12b-2 filer status.

key_terms.definition: An issuer that is neither a large accelerated nor an accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2.
The outside audit firm's report on internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b).

subtopics.memory_aid: 404(c) cuts the auditor's b, never management's a.

subtopics.name: Dodd-Frank Changes to Section 806
subtopics.definition: Dodd-Frank amended Section 806 to lengthen the complaint deadline, add jury trials, cover subsidiaries and rating agencies, and void waivers and predispute arbitration agreements.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These changes made SOX whistleblower claims easier to bring and harder to sign away. Exam items often test the old version against the current one.
how_it_works: Section 922(c) raised the deadline from 90 to 180 days and let it run from when the employee learns of the violation (1514A(b)(2)(D)).
It added a right to a jury trial when the employee takes the claim to federal court (1514A(b)(2)(E)).
It added subsection (e): Section 806 rights cannot be waived by any agreement, policy or condition of employment.
Under the same subsection, no predispute arbitration agreement is valid if it requires arbitrating a Section 806 dispute.
Section 929A covered subsidiaries and affiliates consolidated into the public company's statements; Section 922(b) added rating organizations.

rows.label: Deadline
cells: 180 days after the violation or after learning of it

rows.label: Covered employers
cells: Plus consolidated subsidiaries, affiliates and rating organizations

subtopics.example: Juniper Analytics, a consolidated subsidiary of a listed insurer, asks every new hire to waive whistleblower claims in exchange for a signing bonus. The parent's general counsel orders the clause removed: Section 806 rights cannot be signed away, and the subsidiary's staff are covered just like the parent's.

review: Inspect employment and severance templates for waiver or arbitration clauses
Confirm subsidiaries' staff receive the same whistleblower notices
evidence: Current offer letter and severance agreement templates
Policy acknowledgments from subsidiary employees
audit_focus.recommend: Have legal counsel remove any clause that waives Section 806 rights or forces their arbitration.
audit_focus.decides: Management removes such clauses; courts refuse to enforce them

subtopics.isaca_rule: Know both versions: the 2002 text gave 90 days; since Dodd-Frank, 180 days from the violation or from learning of it, a jury in court, consolidated subsidiaries covered, and no waiver or predispute arbitration of Section 806 rights.

exam_traps.trap: An employee who signed an arbitration agreement at hiring must arbitrate a Section 806 claim.
exam_traps.why: Since Dodd-Frank, a predispute arbitration agreement is not valid or enforceable for a Section 806 dispute.

exam_traps.trap: Section 806 does not reach a public company's subsidiaries.
exam_traps.why: Section 929A added subsidiaries and affiliates whose financial information is consolidated into the public company's statements.

key_terms.definition: An agreement, made before any dispute arises, to resolve future disputes by arbitration instead of in court.
Giving up a legal right, usually in an agreement; Section 806 rights cannot be waived.

subtopics.memory_aid: After 2010: 180 days, a jury, no waiver, no forced arbitration.

subtopics.name: Clawback Policies Under Rule 10D-1
subtopics.definition: Rule 10D-1, adopted under Dodd-Frank Section 954, requires listed issuers to recover erroneously awarded incentive pay from executive officers after an accounting restatement, regardless of fault.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Executives should not keep pay earned on wrong numbers. The rule is easy to confuse with SOX Section 304, which is narrower and needs misconduct.
how_it_works: Exchanges must refuse to list issuers that lack a compliant written recovery policy (17 CFR 240.10D-1(a)).
A restatement to correct a material error, or one that would cause a material misstatement if left uncorrected, triggers recovery (10D-1(b)(1)).
The policy covers incentive pay received by current or former executive officers in the three completed fiscal years before the restatement date (10D-1(b)(1)(i)).
Only the excess over what the restated numbers would have paid is recovered, computed without regard to taxes (10D-1(b)(1)(iii)).
Recovery applies regardless of fault (SEC Release No. 33-11126), and the issuer may not indemnify executives against it (10D-1(b)(1)(v)).
Narrow exceptions apply where independent directors find recovery impracticable, such as costs exceeding the amount (10D-1(b)(1)(iv)).

rows.label: Who repays
cells: All current and former executive officers

rows.label: Trigger
cells: Restatement due to material noncompliance, no fault needed

rows.label: Look-back
cells: Three completed fiscal years before the restatement date

rows.label: What is repaid
cells: Bonuses, incentive pay and stock-sale profits
Incentive pay above the restated amount

subtopics.example: Arden Hotels finds a lease accounting mistake made in good faith and corrects two years of results. The compensation committee works out, officer by officer, how much earnings-based pay would not have been earned on the corrected numbers, and sends repayment demands, with no exceptions for officers who had no part in the mistake.

review: Compare the recovery policy's terms with Rule 10D-1's requirements
Reperform the excess-pay calculation for a sample of executive officers
evidence: Board-approved written recovery policy filed as required
Recovery calculations and repayment records after any restatement
audit_focus.recommend: Have the compensation committee recover excess incentive pay promptly after any required restatement, without regard to fault.
audit_focus.decides: Independent directors decide any impracticability exception

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rule 10D-1 is no-fault and broad: every executive officer, three completed fiscal years before the restatement date, only the excess pay, and no indemnity. Section 304 is narrower: CEO and CFO, misconduct, 12 months.

exam_traps.trap: A clawback under Rule 10D-1 requires executive misconduct.
exam_traps.why: Recovery applies regardless of fault; misconduct is the trigger only under SOX Section 304.

exam_traps.trap: The issuer recovers the whole bonus.
exam_traps.why: Only the amount above what the restated results would have paid is recovered.

key_terms.definition: Incentive pay received above what would have been paid had it been based on the restated numbers.
Pay granted, earned or vested based wholly or partly on a financial reporting measure.
Under Rule 10D-1, the president, principal financial and accounting officers, vice-presidents running principal business units, and other policy makers.

subtopics.memory_aid: 10D-1: no fault, all executives, three years, excess only.

key_terminologies.Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC): The federal agency created by the 1934 Act that writes securities rules and enforces the securities laws, including SOX.
key_terminologies.Securities Act of 1933: The law governing offers and sales of securities: registration, prospectus disclosure and antifraud.
key_terminologies.Securities Exchange Act of 1934: The law that created the SEC and governs trading, market firms and periodic reports.
key_terminologies.Notice and comment: The rulemaking steps of publishing a proposed rule and taking public comments before adopting it.
key_terminologies.Formal order of investigation: A Commission order giving named staff subpoena power in an investigation.
key_terminologies.Wells notice: A staff notice that it plans to recommend charges, with a chance to respond first.
key_terminologies.Section 1519: The SOX-created crime of destroying or falsifying records to obstruct a federal matter, up to 20 years.
key_terminologies.Rule 2-06: The SEC rule requiring an issuer's auditor to keep audit and review records for seven years.
key_terminologies.Nondischargeable debt: A debt that survives bankruptcy, as securities fraud debts do under Section 803.
key_terminologies.Section 806: The SOX protection against retaliation for employees who report fraud, enforced through the Secretary of Labor.
key_terminologies.Original information: A whistleblower's own knowledge or analysis that the SEC does not already have.
key_terminologies.Investor Protection Fund: The SEC fund that pays Dodd-Frank whistleblower awards.
key_terminologies.Section 1349: The SOX-created rule that attempts and conspiracies carry the same penalties as the fraud offense.
key_terminologies.Financial Stability Oversight Council (F: The Dodd-Frank council, chaired by the Treasury Secretary, that watches system-wide financial risk.
key_terminologies.Orderly liquidation authority: The Dodd-Frank Title II process for winding down failing financial companies without taxpayer losses.
key_terminologies.Federal Insurance Office: A Treasury office that monitors insurance but does not regulate insurers.
key_terminologies.Volcker Rule: Dodd-Frank Section 619's limits on banking entities' proprietary trading and hedge or private equity fund stakes.
key_terminologies.Section 404(c): The Dodd-Frank exemption of non-accelerated filers from the auditor's internal control attestation.
key_terminologies.Predispute arbitration agreement: An agreement made before any dispute to arbitrate future claims; unenforceable for Section 806 claims.
key_terminologies.Rule 10D-1: The SEC rule requiring listed issuers to claw back incentive pay after a restatement, without regard to fault.
